# Assignment


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

`←` assigns the value to its right to the target, the
[run](terms.qmd#term-run) just before it. Besides plain names, a target
can be a selection, a dot path, a subscript or a list of names. With a
function just before `←`, as in `x+←1`, the assignment is modified. For
the exact rules, see [Assign](glyphs/left-arrow.qmd) and
[Syntax](syntax.qmd#assignment).

## Plain assignment

`x←Y` binds `x` to `Y` and returns `Y` without displaying it:

``` bpl
x←3
x+2
```

    5

A value can be a function, such as `+/`:

``` bpl
sum←+/
sum 1 2 3
```

    6

Assignments can be chained:

``` bpl
a←b←3
a+b
```

    6

Put independent assignments on separate lines, or put `◇` between them,
because `←` takes everything to its right:

``` bpl
p←1 q←2
p
```

    1 2

`_←Y` evaluates `Y` and discards its value.

## Modified assignment

`x f←Y` sets `x` to `x f Y`:

``` bpl
x+←3
x
```

    6

Any function works, such as `,` to append:

``` bpl
s←"abc"
s,←"d"
s
```

    "abcd"

To modify with a named function, write `x⁝f←Y`, which means `x←x f Y`.
In `x f←Y`, the target would be `f`:

``` bpl
f←×
x⁝f←4
x
```

    24

With nothing after the arrow, modified assignment applies the function
to the target alone. `x⌽←` sets `x` to `⌽x`:

``` bpl
x←1 2 3
x⌽←
x
```

    3 2 1

## Assigning to part of an array

Assigning to a [subscript](scripts.ipynb#subscripts) target replaces the
item at one literal position:

``` bpl
v←1 2 3
v₁←9
v
```

    1 9 3

Use dot brackets to select any positions, in plain or modified
assignment:

``` bpl
v.[[0 2]]+←10
v
```

    11 9 13

For any other selection, put the target in parentheses and use a
function that only selects or rearranges, as for structural
[Under](glyphs/at.qmd):

``` bpl
(2↑v)←8 9
v
```

    8 9 13

A dfn that returns items of its argument can be the selection too. A
space before `←` makes the whole run the target:

``` bpl
{ω.[⍸ω>8]}v ←0
v
```

    8 0 0

The selection can apply a function with rank. `0⌷¹` selects the first
item of each row:

``` bpl
M←[1 2
   3 4]
(0⌷¹ M)←9
M
```

    9 2
    9 4

Assign to a dot path to write a field of a record:

``` bpl
T←["n":1]
T.n+←1
T.n
```

    2

A plain assignment to a dot path creates any missing records along the
path:

``` bpl
T.addr.city←"SF"
T
```

    ["n":2 "addr":["city":"SF"]]

A subscript can follow a dot path:

``` bpl
T.a←1 2
T.a₁←7
T.a
```

    1 7

## Inverses and derivatives

`f⁻←g` attaches `g` as the inverse of the function named by `f`. `f⁻`,
negative [powers](glyphs/star-diaeresis.qmd) and [Under](glyphs/at.qmd)
then call `g`:

``` bpl
inc←1+
inc⁻←¯1+
inc⍣¯2⁝5
```

    3

`f∂←g` attaches `g` as the derivative of `f`, which
[`∂`](glyphs/partial.qmd) and [`⇄`](glyphs/right-left-arrows.qmd) call.
`g` is a JVP rule: `t g x` gives the derivative of `f` at `x` along the
direction `t`, and must be linear in `t`. `∂` calls `g` wherever it
differentiates a call of `f`:

``` bpl
sq←{ω×ω}
sq∂←{α×2×ω}
sq∂3
```

    6

Calling the function still runs its original definition. Assigning an
inverse does not change its derivative rule, and assigning a derivative
does not change its inverse:

``` bpl
sq⁻←√
[sq 3;sq∂ 3;sq⁻ 9]
```

    9 6 3

## Destructuring

A list of names in brackets destructures a value by position:

``` bpl
[a b]←10 20
a+b
```

    30

Each name is assigned one major cell of a higher-rank value, such as one
row of a matrix:

``` bpl
[top bottom]←2 3ρι6ₓ
bottom
```

    [3 4 5]ₓ

A single value goes to every name:

``` bpl
[c d]←5
c d
```

    5 5

A nested list of names destructures a nested value:

``` bpl
[e [g h]]←[1 [2 3]]
h
```

    3

Modified assignment works on a list of names too:

``` bpl
[a b]+←10
a b
```

    20 30

Inside brackets, every name is a target, even one that holds a function,
such as `f`:

``` bpl
[f n]←1 2
f
```

    1

A list of names destructures by position even when the value has keys. A
pattern destructures by key instead. Each cell of a pattern is a key,
then the name that is assigned the key’s item, as in `[a:x]`. A cell
with only a key, as in `[a:]`, assigns the item to the name spelled like
the key. A key is never a value: the `a` in `[a:x]` stands for the key
`"a"`, whatever `a` holds. Use a string key, as in `["first name":n]`,
when the key isn’t a valid name. The cells can come in any order:

``` bpl
[b: a:x]←["a":1 "b":2 "c":3]
x b
```

    1 2

A program takes names from a [module](modules.qmd) this way, as in
`[disp:]←•load "lib/array.bpl"`.

## Names inside dfns

Inside a dfn, plain assignment makes a local name:

``` bpl
total←0
set←{total←ω ◇ total}
_←set 5
total
```

    0

Modified and selective assignment, including assigning an inverse or
derivative, update the nearest existing binding, even outside the dfn:

``` bpl
add←{total+←ω ◇ total}
_←add 5
total
```

    5

Arrays have value semantics, as numbers do:

``` bpl
u←1 2
w←u
u₀←9
w
```

    1 2

An array is copied only when it is modified while another name or array
holds it. Above, `u₀←9` copies `u` first, because `w` holds it too.
Assigning to part of an array that nothing else holds changes the array
in place. `x,←v` and `x⍪←v` add to the end of the array’s storage.
`x←x,v` always copies, because `x` still holds the old array while `x,v`
is computed.
